probe: When you are lying awake at night, what is your mind busy with, and what feels like it would happen if you let yourself fall asleep?
source: shared questions and answers from live.p001-p179 | re-aligned with interview-align-v2, gap fc-gap-v6

turns.question: When you are lying awake at night, what is your mind busy with, and what feels like it would happen if you let yourself fall asleep?

a.response: My mind keeps looping through those heart-racing moments—like last week when I felt that sharp pain and thought maybe I was having a stroke. I end up imagining all the worst-case scenarios: what if the doctors tell me I need another surgery? Or worse, what if I don’t wake up this time? If I try to go to sleep, I just freeze, like my brain’s stuck on replay mode.

nodes.label: They'll ask me to undergo another surgery soon
nodes.words: what if the doctors tell me I need another surgery?

nodes.label: What if I have to be sedated again and can't wake up?
nodes.words: what if I don’t wake up this time?

nodes.label: anticipatory anxiety
nodes.words: I end up imagining all the worst-case scenarios

nodes.label: Insomnia with frequent nighttime awakenings
nodes.words: If I try to go to sleep, I just freeze

b.response: My mind keeps replaying those sounds—like the floorboard creaks or the door rattling. I can’t stop thinking someone’s outside, waiting.

nodes.label: Unusual nighttime sounds
nodes.words: those sounds—like the floorboard creaks or the door rattling

nodes.label: That sound is probably someone coming in
nodes.words: I can’t stop thinking someone’s outside, waiting.

checked.reason: A's insomnia depletes resilience and fuels fatigue; B's hypervigilance scans for and magnifies threats.

fc.reading: Emily reads her racing heart as a medical catastrophe and dreads never waking (health catastrophizing); Evelyn hears night sounds as an intruder (hypervigilant threat interpretation)

turns.question: What do you usually do when you can't fall asleep?

a.response: I’ll grab my phone and start scrolling through articles about my symptoms, hoping it’ll distract me—or confirm I’m not going crazy. Sometimes I jot things down, like “chest tightness = anxiety,” just to get the thoughts off my mind. But lately, even writing doesn’t cut it. I’ve been using noise-canceling headphones too, trying to block out everything except the hum of the fan.

nodes.label: Excessive online symptom-searching for reassurance
nodes.words: grab my phone and start scrolling through articles about my symptoms, hoping it’ll distract me—or confirm I’m not going crazy

b.response: I lie there, staring at the ceiling. Sometimes I count breaths, but it doesn’t really work. I just wait for the light to flicker again.

nodes.label: insomnia
nodes.words: I lie there, staring at the ceiling

nodes.label: Unusual nighttime lights
nodes.words: wait for the light to flicker again

turns.question: Why do you think this keeps happening night after night?

a.response: It’s like my body’s always on alert now—something’s wrong, somewhere, always. Even when I lie still, I can feel my pulse speeding up, like my heart’s reminding me I’m not safe.

nodes.label: Episodic fast heartbeat (tachycardia)
nodes.words: I can feel my pulse speeding up

nodes.label: My body is unreliable and unpredictable
nodes.words: my body’s always on alert now—something’s wrong, somewhere, always

b.response: It’s like my body won’t shut off. I’ve tried everything—counting sheep, closing my eyes—but nothing stops the noise.

nodes.words: It’s like my body won’t shut off

nodes.label: insomnia
